messages.subject: coding random slope model (with or without an uncorrelated random intercept)
messages.subject_clean: coding random slope model (with or without an uncorrelated random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is there a simple way of coding random slope model with INLA?

For exemple, if I want to include a random slope in my model for a contious variable "x" that varies in different "region".

With the package LME4, a code like this would do the job:

y ~ x + (0+x|region)

If I wanted to include an uncorrelated random intercept, it will become y ~ x + (1|region) + (0+x|region)

Could I reproduce these models with INLA? if yes, how?

Best regards,

Julien

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 2011-04-06 at 12:13 -0700, Julien wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Is there a simple way of coding random slope model with INLA?
>
> For exemple, if I want to include a random slope in my model for a
> contious variable "x" that varies in different "region".
>
> With the package LME4, a code like this would do the job:
>
> y ~ x + (0+x|region)
>
> If I wanted to include an uncorrelated random intercept, it will
> become y ~ x + (1|region) + (0+x|region)
>
> Could I reproduce these models with INLA? if yes, how?
>
> Best regards,
>
> Julien

I presumed you ment that you wanted to correlated the intercept and the
slope, but if you do not want that, then

	f(region, covariate, model ="iid")

is a random slope model, where

	region[i] is the region for data y[i]
	covariate[i] is the covariate for data y[i]

so that this gives with z = covariate,

	+ \beta_region * z_i ....

the second argument in f() is an optional weight for the f-term.

H

messages.subject: Recent changes
messages.subject_clean: Recent changes
messages.body_plain:
In this first email, I just to make you aware of some recent changes
and developments that you may or may not find useful.  Some of them
refer to the testing-version of the code, which you can obtain with

    inla.upgrade(testing=TRUE)

Some recent (larger) changes and stuff in development:

* Finn Lindgren has reimplemented the interface toward to the
spde-based models; see for example the example at

http://www.r-inla.org/examples/case-studies/lindgren-rue-and-lindstrom-rss-paper-2011
the basic functionallity is there, but the interface is not yet
finished. there is more to come.

*  The pdf-documentation found on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> is now available locally
as well. A prototype of this functionallity is

    inla.doc("rw2")

which display the pdf documentation for the rw2 model, and so with all
latent, likelihood and prior models. The pdf-doc is stored locally so
you do not need to be online.

* Various link-functions are now available; see

    http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-Does-INLA-support-the-use-of-differ

* A call to `inla.hyperpar' return now the same object-type as a call
to inla(), only that the marginals for the hyperparamters are updated
(and so with the marginal likelihood estimates)

* A new system for setting priors, parameters, initial values for
hyperparameters has been implemented. However, this new system is
backward compatible with the old prior=,param=,fixed=,initial=, way of
doing it. The examples are (or should be) updated. See ?inla.models

* The internal storage of the results from the linear combinations, in

    r = inla(..., lincomb=lc)

has changed, and they are all stored in a matrix.

* Another layer of linear predictor's has been added, see

http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools#TOC-Models-where-the-response-data-depe

which makes it much easier to implement certain models.

* If you have a graph-spesification in a file, and there is an error in
it, then you can use inla.debug.graph("file.graph")  to read it with
extensive checking along the way, so that the error can be detected
(hopefully). also plotting of graphs is supported, with

    g = inla.read.graph("file.graph")
    plot(g)

which require the `Rgraphviz' (from the Bioconductor package). I don't
know if this feature is useful, but its kind of fun.

*  the models "besag", "besag2" and "bym", now automatically check if
the graph has more than  one connected component. [It seems to be more
common than I  thought initially...]. And if so, the interpretation of
the `constr=TRUE' is interpreted as one linear constraint on each
connected component, and the rank-deficiancy is adjusted similarly.
This is the correct way to do it, as its implicitely assumed that the
graph has only one connected component.

I think that was more or less the most important changes during the
last 2-3 months.

I almost forgot, we have started a discussion group at r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>

http://www.r-inla.org/comments-1
so that questions posted there can be answered by any, and the
discussion might be useful for others as well.

Best,
H

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Havard for your previous response. It is now clear to me how to code a random slope model. However, I had trouble to obtain convergence with a simple random intercept model (see below) whereas it worked fine using lme4 package (see below). Also, I have tried to code a combined random intercept-slope model (see below) in INLA using the copy function that you mentioned in your previous message but I did not have any success. Could you indicate how to replicate the following models (fitted with lme4 packages) using the simulated data set below?

Thank you for your time,

Julien

########################

## Simulated data set ##

########################

x <- sort(unique(runif(100, 0, 20)))

y1 <- 60 - 2*x + rnorm(length(x), 0, 4)

y2 <- 70 - 0.6*x + rnorm(length(x), 0, 4)

y3 <- 45 + 1*x + rnorm(length(x), 0, 4)

y4 <- 35 + 1.3*x + rnorm(length(x), 0, 4)

plot(x,y1, ylim=c(20,80), xlim=c(0,30))

points(x, y2, col="red")

points(x, y3, col="green")

points(x, y4, col="orange")

abline(a=coef(lm(y1~x))[1], b=coef(lm(y1~x))[2])

abline(a=coef(lm(y2~x))[1], b=coef(lm(y2~x))[2])

abline(a=coef(lm(y3~x))[1], b=coef(lm(y3~x))[2])

abline(a=coef(lm(y4~x))[1], b=coef(lm(y4~x))[2])

mydata <- data.frame(x1 = rep(x, times = 4), y = c(y1,y2,y3,y4), bloc = rep(c(1,2,3,4), each = length(x)), fuzzy = rep(1, 400))

##########

## LME4 ##

##########

require(lme4)

# no random effect

model_no_random <- lmer( y ~ x1 + (1|fuzzy), data = mydata)

summary(model_no_random)

# random intercept only

model_intercept <- lmer( y ~ x1 + (1|bloc), data = mydata)

summary(model_intercept)

# random slope only

model_slope <- lmer( y ~ x1 + (0 + x1|bloc), data = mydata)

summary(model_slope)

# random slope of x1 within bloc with correlated intercept

model_slope_intercept_correlated <- lmer( y ~ x1 + (x1|bloc), data = mydata)

summary(model_slope_intercept_correlated)

# uncorrelated random intercept and random slope within bloc

model_slope_intercept_uncorrelated <- lmer(y ~ x1 + (1|bloc) + (0 + x1|bloc), data = mydata)

summary(model_slope_intercept_uncorrelated)

##########

## INLA ##

##########

require(INLA)

# no random effect

formule_no_random = y ~ x1

model_no_random_INLA = inla.cpo(formula=formule_no_random, data=mydata, family="gaussian", control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

summary(model_no_random_INLA)

# random intercept only

formule_random_intercept_only = y ~ x1 + f(bloc, model = "iid")

model_random_intecept_only_INLA = inla.cpo(formula=formule_random_intercept_only, data=mydata, family="gaussian", control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

summary(model_random_intecept_only_INLA)

# random slope only

formule_random_slope_only = y ~ x1 + f(bloc, x1, model = "iid")

model_random_slope_only_INLA = inla.cpo(formula=formule_random_slope_only, data=mydata, family="gaussian", control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

summary(model_random_slope_only_INLA)

# random slope of x1 within bloc with correlated intercept

formule_random_correlated_intercept_slope = y ~ x1 + ?

model_random_correlated_intercept_slope_INLA = inla.cpo(formula=formule_random_correlated_intercept_slope, data=mydata, family="gaussian", control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

summary(model_random_correlated_intercept_slope_INLA)

# uncorrelated random intercept and random slope within bloc

formule_random_uncorrelated_intercept_slope = y ~ x1 + ?

model_random_uncorrelated_intercept_slope_INLA = inla.cpo(formula=formule_random_uncorrelated_intercept_slope, data=mydata, family="gaussian", control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

Hi,

you're almost there...

	result$marginals.hyperpar

is a list of marginals. you just have to pick the right one.

the new names for transforming marginals and computing expectations, are
inla.tmarginal() and inla.emarginal().

hopefully this example will clarify the issue.

best,
H

n = 10
y = rnorm(n)
i = 1:n
r = inla(y~1+f(i, model="iid"), data = data.frame(i, y))

print(names(r$marginals.hyperpar))

marg.variance = inla.tmarginal(
        function(x) 1/x,
        r$marginals.hyperpar$'Precision for i')

plot(inla.spline(marg.variance))
m = inla.emarginal(function(x) x, marg.variance)
mm = inla.emarginal(function(x) x^2, marg.variance)

print(paste("mean", m))
print(paste("sd",  sqrt(mm-m^2)))

On Mon, 2011-04-18 at 11:39 -0700, marcelo....@hotmail.com wrote:
> Attached are sending a paper titled "Stochastic super-resolution image
> reconstruction" of Jing Tian, Kai-Kuang Ma, 2010.
>
> In this article, the authors, in section 2, mathematically model the
> problem of superresolution. Moreover, a solution is
> developed using MCMC.
>
>
> I would like to use INLA in place of MCMC. Is it possible?
>
> Sincerely,
>

Hi.

I have read the paper: yes you can.

However, I would rather recommend to code this yourself (in matlab/R),
as this is tricky using inla() and you'll get an overhead
computationally, due to the internal representation.

Further, the model in the paper is rather easy and you can derive a
very very quick (exact up the 1d integration error) algorithm using
discrete Fourier Transforms (DFT). Note that the posterior, for fixed
\lambda, is Gaussian. Just make cyclic boundary conditions (wrap the
image on the torus),  then the precision matrix is Toeplitz circulant
and you can compute the mean and marginal variance using DFT.  also the
eigenvalues \lamda_min/max, can be computed using DFT.  Then use the
INLA-idea with Gaussian approximation only (sec 3.2.1 in the inla
paper), which is exact in this case, since x|y,\theta, *is* gaussian.

The DFT stuff is spelled out in section 2.6 in the GMRF book,
otherwise, you can find it elsewhere as well.

hope this helps.

H

messages.body_plain:
Hi Havard, thanks for the quick response.

I think I see now....  A couple comments...

1) so you report the posterior for theta2 (the reparameterization of
xi) but the posterior for the original tau (i.e., not theta1)?  In the
example the posterior mean for the precision is about 4 which is the
true tau, not theta1.  That was part of my confusion - I saw that tau
was reported (the original parameterization) and therefore assumed xi
was reported.

2) I think that prior on xi as the default might be fairly narrow, but
don't have a lot of experience with GEVs either.  But for
precipitation extremes, my sense is that that prior is too narrow.
Obviously the user can change it and something has to be the default
though.

Chris

>> normal with mean 0 and sd .01*sqrt(1/6.25) = .004.  This seems quite
>> restrictive and in the example fit shown in the documentation, I
>> actually get a posterior  for what appears to be xi that has 95% CI of

>> prior.  Am I missing something or is there a typo in the

you can either add it generally

inla(...., quantiles = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9))
